Note
nōt
v. and n. (to mark down, to set a mark upon; also a mark of distinction, as of note)
Latin nota, a mark, a sign, a written character. The verb runs two ways in Scripture: to write a thing down so that it stands for the time to come, and to mark a man out for the church's discipline.

Definition · Scriptures · Corruption · Roots · Usage · Related

Biblical Definition

Isaiah is commanded to make a record that will outlive him: “Now go, write it before them in a table, and note it in a book, that it may be for the time to come for ever and ever” (Isa 30:8). Habakkuk receives the same charge in different words: “Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it” (Hab 2:2). Prophecy is committed to writing on purpose, so that a later generation can check what was said against what came — the whole doctrine of an inscripturated word is present in the command. The second use is the church's: “And if any man obey not our word by this epistle, note that man, and have no company with him, that he may be ashamed” (2Th 3:14). Here noting is the congregation marking a disobedient brother, and the stated aim is not his destruction but his shame unto repentance — the next verse forbids counting him an enemy and requires admonishing him as a brother. A third sense is honour: Andronicus and Junia are “of note among the apostles” (Rom 16:7). Scripture notes men down for warning and for honour, and it does both in writing.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a note as a mark or token; a character or sign; a short writing or memorandum; and to note as to observe carefully, to mark, or to set down in writing.

expand to see more

NOTE, n. [L. nota.] A mark or token; something by which a thing may be known; a visible sign.

2. A short writing; a memorandum; a minute.

3. Reputation; consequence; distinction; as men of note.

NOTE, v.t. To observe; to notice with particular care; to heed; to attend to. Note that man, and have no company with him. 2 Thess. iii.

Key Scripture

Isa 30:8 — "Now go, write it before them in a table, and note it in a book, that it may be for the time to come for ever and ever:"

Hab 2:2 — "And the LORD answered me, and said, Write the vision, and make it plain upon tables, that he may run that readeth it."

2Th 3:14 — "And if any man obey not our word by this epistle, note that man, and have no company with him, that he may be ashamed."

Rom 16:7 — "Salute Andronicus and Junia, my kinsmen, and my fellowprisoners, who are of note among the apostles, who also were in Christ before me."

Modern Corruption

The apostolic command to note a disobedient man is now felt to be unloving, though Paul gives the aim in the same sentence — that he may be ashamed — and forbids treating him as an enemy in the next.

expand to see more

Church discipline has quietly fallen out of use in most congregations, and where it is mentioned it is defended or attacked in terms Paul never uses. The command at 2 Thessalonians 3:14 is short and unembarrassed: note that man, and have no company with him. Two things are worth marking. The first is that the ground is disobedience to apostolic teaching, not personality, not preference, and not a quarrel with the leadership; discipline that is used to protect a pastor's position rather than the church's obedience is the abuse, and the abuse does not abolish the ordinance. The second is that the aim is stated: that he may be ashamed. Shame is not here a wound inflicted for its own sake but the God-given pain by which a man who has grown comfortable in sin is made uncomfortable enough to return, and the very next verse guards it — count him not as an enemy, but admonish him as a brother.

The other half of the word bears on how we hold the Scriptures themselves. Isaiah is told to note it in a book, that it may be for the time to come. The written form is not a lesser vehicle than the spoken one; it is given precisely so the word can be examined by generations that never heard the prophet's voice. That cuts against the notion, common wherever fresh revelation is claimed, that the living voice in the room outranks the settled text — the prophets themselves were sent to the book. It also puts a duty on the reader. A written word can be checked, and Habakkuk says it is made plain so that he may run that readeth it: plain enough to be understood, and public enough that no man needs an authorised interpreter standing between him and the page.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew chaqaq (H2710), to inscribe or engrave, rendered note at Isaiah 30:8; Greek semeioo (G4593), to mark or signify, at 2 Thessalonians 3:14; episemos (G1978), of note, bearing a mark.

expand to see more

Hebrew chaqaq (H2710) — to cut in, to inscribe, to decree; note it in a book for the time to come; Isaiah 30:8.

Hebrew baar (H874) — to make plain or distinct; make it plain upon tables; Habakkuk 2:2, Deuteronomy 27:8.

Greek semeioo (G4593) — to mark, to set a sign upon; note that man; 2 Thessalonians 3:14.

Greek episemos (G1978) — bearing a mark, notable, of note; used of Andronicus and Junia and of Barabbas; Romans 16:7, Matthew 27:16.

Greek noutheteo (G3560) — to admonish, to put in mind; the treatment prescribed for the noted brother; 2 Thessalonians 3:15.

Usage

"“Note it in a book, that it may be for the time to come” — prophecy committed to writing on purpose."

"“Note that man… that he may be ashamed” — the discipline whose aim is stated in the same breath."

"“Of note among the apostles” — the same word for honour."
